newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. promises investment to reward Africa reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. promises investment to reward Africa reforms.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Thursday the superpower would direct trade and investment towards African countries committed to economic reform, but would not pour in unlimited aid.
Summers, in an address to the Johannesburg-based Wits Business School, said a generational leadership shift and economic realism had left a sense of progress on the continent.

"I believe that the prospects for economic growth in the developing countries of Africa are the brightest they've been in a generation," said Summers, on a week-long tour of Africa and his first visit to South Africa.
"We (the U.S.) believe that the best prospects for making a positive contribution to economic development in Africa lie in reinforcing strong reform where it is taking place.
"The partnership we propose emphasises selectivity, the importance of international integration, private capital over official grants and the role of markets in driving development."
Summers said the U.S. would not limit the number of nations it admitted to the "club of reformers" in Africa which it hoped to reward with trade and investment.
"There's no quota on admissions to this 'club'. We are prepared to extend special trade benefits, extra finance, to any countries that are prepared to take the steps necessary to qualify for it."

Summers referred to an initiative announced last month for the U.S. Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) to launch a $150 million fund for equity investment in Africa in a number of sectors -- two thirds of it consisting of OPIC-guaranteed debt. He said it would be based in Johannesburg.
Details of the first fund are still being finalised, but Summers said a second OPIC fund, to be capitalised at $500 million, was being prepared and would focus on infrastructural development.
"Countries pursuing the deepest market-oriented reforms are likely to capture the lion's share of the investments," he said.
